extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when subject matter that would otherwise be prior art is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) because of common ownership or a joint research agreement, and the procedural steps/evidence required to invoke that disqualification during examination, reexamination, or reissue. Includes applicability, timing, required statements, and examiner responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) prior art disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter which qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) shall not be used to reject a claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention "were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies only to prior art usable in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; subject matter that qualifies as anticipatory prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 is not affected and may still be used to reject claims as anticipated. Double patenting rejections based on subject matter disqualified under 103(c) should still be made as appropriate. The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art is placed on the person urging disqualification once the examiner has established a prima facie case of obviousness based on the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement (JRA) safe-harbor requirements (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2)/(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103, subject matter developed by another person and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The JRA must be a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. The JRA must be in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made (it need not be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference sought to be disqualified). To invoke this safe harbor, applicants must comply with statute and rules of practice (see 37 CFR 1.71(g) and 1.104(c)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "joint research agreement"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Joint research agreement" means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3)) is used for determining eligibility for the JRA safe harbor; the JRA must have been in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "commonly owned" for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term "commonly owned" is intended to mean that the subject matter which would otherwise be prior art to the claimed invention and the claimed invention are entirely or wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s)/business entity(ies). For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), common ownership must be at the time the claimed invention was made. If the person(s) or organization(s) owned less than 100 percent of the subject matter or less than 100 percent of the claimed invention, then common ownership would not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership requires 100% ownership of both the reference subject matter and the claimed invention at the time the later invention was made. A license of the claimed invention to another by the owner where basic ownership rights are retained would not defeat ownership. The question is determined on the facts of the particular case; moral or unenforceable obligations do not evidence common ownership. Present statements of ownership are insufficient—ownership must be shown to have existed at the time the invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence sufficient to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and references will be considered by the examiner to be owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, at the time the invention was made, if the applicant(s) or an attorney or agent of record makes a statement to the effect that the application and the reference were, at the time the invention was made, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant's or representative's statement is sufficient because of their paramount obligation of candor and good faith to the USPTO. The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on a separate piece of paper or in a separately labeled section) so the examiner notices it. Applicants may but are not required to submit further evidence such as recorded assignments, copies of unrecorded assignments, affidavits/declarations by the common owner, or court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence the examiner may require when representation is doubted
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare instances the examiner may have independent evidence that raises a material doubt as to the accuracy of applicant's representation of common ownership or existence of an obligation to commonly assign; in such cases the examiner may explain the doubt and require objective evidence of common ownership or obligation to assign as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable objective evidence includes: (A) reference to assignments recorded in the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office conveying entire rights to the same person(s); (B) copies of unrecorded assignments conveying entire rights filed in each application; (C) an affidavit or declaration by the common owner stating common ownership and explaining facts supporting it, signed by an official empowered to act for the organization; and (D) other evidence establishing common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and examiner's prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art is placed on the person urging that the subject matter is disqualified (e.g., the applicant or patentee) once the examiner has established a prima facie case of obviousness based on the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that a reference and the application have the same assignee is not, by itself, sufficient evidence to disqualify the prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c); there must be a statement that common ownership existed 'at the time the invention was made.' It would not be appropriate to place the burden upon the patent examiner or the defendant in litigation; the applicant/patentee is expected to have the relevant evidence if it exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and effective date rules for the CREATE Act amendment to 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act amended 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and is effective for patents granted on or after December 10, 2004. The amendment applies to all applications pending on or after December 10, 2004, including those filed prior to November 29, 1999. The amendment does not affect any application filed before November 29, 1999 and issued as a patent prior to December 10, 2004, nor final decisions rendered before December 10, 2004.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reexamination proceedings, whether 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended applies depends on whether the patent being reexamined was granted on or after December 10, 2004. For patents granted prior to December 10, 2004 on applications filed on or after November 29, 1999, the 1999 changes to 103(c) are applicable; for patents granted prior to December 10, 2004 on applications filed prior to November 29, 1999, neither the 1999 nor the 2004 changes apply. The CREATE Act amendments continue to apply only to prior art under 102(e), (f), or (g) relied upon in a 103 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for amending specification to disclose JRA parties (37 CFR 1.71(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification may disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to a joint research agreement (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2)(C)). An amendment under 1.71(g)(1) must be accompanied by the processing fee set forth in 1.17(i) if not filed within certain time periods (within three months of national filing date; within three months of national stage entry; before mailing of first Office action on the merits; or before mailing of first Office action after RCE). If an amendment under 1.71(g)(1) is filed after the issue fee is paid, the patent as issued may not include the names; correction must be by certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 1.323.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unnecessary to file a reissue or request reexamination solely to submit the amendment and invoke 103(c) if the patent was granted on or after December 10, 2004. The submission is subject to other rules (1.116, 1.121, 1.312). If the amendment is submitted in an application under final rejection to overcome a 103(a) rejection based on a U.S. patent available only under 102(e), the examiner may refuse to enter the amendment if it is not accompanied by an appropriate terminal disclaimer (1.321(d)) because the amendment may necessitate reopening prosecution and introduce double patenting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required statement content, location, and signature (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4) and practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome a 103(a) rejection based on subject matter qualifying under 102(e), (f), or (g) via 103(c)(2), the applicant must provide a statement to the effect that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should either be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)). The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). When an applicant disqualifies subject matter and follows the rules, the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as if commonly owned for purposes of 103(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner actions and examination consequences when 103(c) is invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant disqualifies the subject matter relied on by the examiner in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and the rules, the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as if they are commonly owned for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must examine the application as to all grounds except 102(e)/(f)/(g) as they apply through 103 only if the file establishes common ownership at the time the later invention was made. The examiner may withdraw a 103(a) rejection and, where appropriate, issue a new double patenting rejection based on the disqualified patent/application publication (which may be made final). Entry of an amendment under 1.71(g) may be refused unless accompanied by a terminal disclaimer when reopening prosecution would be necessitated. Rejections based on anticipation under 102 remain available; double patenting issues and terminal disclaimers may arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an invention is "made" (timing of common ownership/JRA effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is 'made' when conception is complete as defined in case law (Mergenthaler v. Scudder; In re Tansel); Pfaff v. Wells Electronics states the invention must be 'ready for patenting' by proof that prior to the critical date the inventor had prepared drawings or other descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership or the JRA must exist on or before the time the later invention was made. The examiner looks to the time at which common ownership exists; ownership obtained after the invention was made cannot be used to disqualify prior art. Common ownership at time of invention may be established irrespective of whether the invention was made in the United States or abroad for purposes of obviating a 103 rejection based on 102(e)/(f)/(g). (Other statutes, e.g., 35 U.S.C. 104 and interference rules, remain applicable for other proceedings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture doctrine caution for reissue applications
rubrics_metrics.description: For reissue applications, the doctrine of recapture may prevent the presentation of claims in the reissue application that were amended or cancelled from the application which matured into the patent, if the claims were amended or cancelled to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) which was not able to be excluded under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) in the original application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner determines this situation applies in the reissue application, consultation with the Office of Patent Legal Administration should be initiated via the Technology Center Special Program Examiner. The CREATE Act's effective date and prior prosecution history can affect recapture analyses.
